solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Movie mogul being choosy?

parts.note: a pic is an informal word for a film or movie
a mogul is a magnate, a king of his industry (a press king, an oil king)

explanation.surface: A film tycoon wondering whether he is being too fussy about scripts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movie mogul' reads as one person, but it splits into two pieces; the question mark flags the loose use of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being selective or fussy describes someone who is choosing carefully, as when a person is picking and choosing.

clue.text: Supported staff under pressure to introduce degree subject

indicators.note: under in a down clue puts the staff below the pressure letter

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for pressure in physics

indicators.note: to introduce says the staff word takes the degree course inside it

parts.note: a rod is a staff or stick
PPE is Philosophy, Politics and Economics, a degree course at Oxford

explanation.surface: A lecturer pressured into bringing in a new course.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'under' means placed below, so P comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Propped means held up or shored up, a synonym for supported by a prop or brace.

clue.text: My work is about helping big business

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like my!

indicators.note: about turns the work letters round

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
a ration is a helping or portion

explanation.surface: Someone saying their job is about helping large companies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is an exclamation, not a possessive: cor! is a British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A corporation is a large company or group of companies acting as one legal entity.

clue.text: Artist accommodated in imposing residence

indicators.note: accommodated in says the answer is lodged within the words imposing residence

explanation.surface: A painter put up in a grand mansion.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres was a French Neoclassical painter, an example of an artist.

clue.text: What's close to hotel, with rough-sounding green expanse?

parts.note: in the NATO phonetic alphabet Golf comes just before Hotel

indicators.note: sounding says the rough word is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: coarse means rough

explanation.surface: Asking what lies near the hotel, with a scrubby lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hotel' is the NATO letter H, next to Golf; 'rough' and 'green' also hint at golf terms.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf course is a large stretch of grassed land laid out for the game, so a green expanse.

clue.text: Here sit and sleep without fuss

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the sleep word wraps round the fuss word

parts.note: to doss is British slang for sleeping rough or bedding down
ado is fuss or bother, as in much ado about nothing

explanation.surface: An invitation to plonk down and nap without any bother.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here, not lacking. A dos-a-dos is a seat on which two people sit back to back, so 'Here sit' describes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dos-a-dos is a back-to-back settee or carriage seat, so it is a place where one would sit.

clue.text: Performance expected on time

parts.note: due means expected, as a train is due

explanation.surface: A show that is due to start on time.
explanation.definitionFit: A duet is a musical piece played or sung by two, a kind of performance.

clue.text: With having to be in school, say, rise and shine

indicators.note: having to be in says the with letter goes inside the school word

parts.note: a school of fish is a shoal
eg, for example, means say

explanation.surface: Pupils told they must be at school, so get up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school' is a school of fish, not a place of lessons. Show a leg is British slang for get out of bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Show a leg is an old naval call meaning get out of bed, the same order as get up.

clue.text: Performed title role in Purcell opera, nothing less

indicators.note: less says the zero letter is taken away

parts.note: Dido is the title role of Purcell's Dido and Aeneas
nothing is zero, which looks like O

explanation.surface: A singer who sang the lead in a Purcell opera, no more.
explanation.definitionFit: Did is the past tense of do, which can mean carried out or performed a task.

clue.text: Heading north, wishes to cross favourite part of London

indicators.note: heading north in a down clue says the whole thing reads upwards, backwards
to cross says the wishes word straddles the favourite word

parts.note: yens are longings or wishes
a pet is a favourite

explanation.surface: Travelling north, hoping to visit a well-loved district of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heading north' reverses YE(PET)NS into STEPNEY, a district in the East End of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Stepney is a district of the East End in the London borough of Tower Hamlets.

clue.text: Take boat to Capri regularly

indicators.note: regularly asks for every other letter of the words to Capri, starting with the second

explanation.surface: Instructions to catch a boat across to the island of Capri.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: in poetic usage the word can be a verb meaning to row, which is to take a boat along.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as a verb in poetry it means to row, propelling a boat by blades, which loosely is taking a boat.

clue.text: Daughters into spinning single record pass on much-loved disc

indicators.note: into says the daughter letter goes inside the reversed pair
spinning turns the single and record words round so they read backwards

parts.note: lone means single or solitary
a log is a record, as in a ship's log
read as Daughter's, daughter is: D is the standard abbreviation for daughter
to pass on is a euphemism for to die

explanation.surface: Daughters spinning a favourite old single on the turntable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daughters' must be read as Daughter's, i.e. daughter is; 'spinning' looks like a turntable but reverses the pair, and 'into' places the D.
explanation.definitionFit: A golden oldie is a hit record from years ago that is still fondly remembered and played.

clue.text: Church backs professional cleric in French region

indicators.note: backs says the church letters come at the back, after the other pieces

parts.note: pro is the short form of professional
Ven, short for Venerable, is the title of an archdeacon
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: The Church supporting a career clergyman somewhere in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backs' looks like support but is a placement signal: CE goes at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Provence is a historic region of south-eastern France, on the Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Kind of emission from vehicle — nut needs turning

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: turning means the head word is read backwards

parts.note: nut and nob are both slang for the head

explanation.surface: A car's exhaust problem traced to a nut that needs tightening.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbon emissions are the carbon dioxide released by burning fuel, so carbon qualifies the noun emission.

clue.text: Scout master ordered opening of presents during Yuletide, once

parts.note: bade, past tense of bid, means ordered

indicators.note: during says that letter sits inside the Christmas word

parts.note: Nowell is an old spelling of Noel, Christmas

indicators.note: opening of asks for the first letter of the word presents

explanation.surface: A troop leader told to open gifts at Christmas long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scout master' is not the troop leader but Robert Baden-Powell, founder of the Scout movement.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Baden-Powell founded the Boy Scouts in 1908, so he is the master of all Scouts.

clue.text: Non-Western writer never turning against religion?

indicators.note: turning says the letters of the shortened writer and never are churned into a new order
Non-Western says the W, for west, is dropped from the writer word

parts.note: taken as written, a writer

explanation.surface: A writer from outside the West who never turns against faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Non-Western' removes W from WRITER, leaving RITER; 'turning' mixes RITER with NEVER. The question mark marks the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Irreverent means disrespectful of sacred things, so showing a lack of respect for religion.

clue.text: Boring research originally introduced by expert

indicators.note: introduced by says the research letter is put inside the expert word

parts.note: a dab, or dab hand, is an expert

indicators.note: originally asks for the opening letter of the word research

explanation.surface: An expert's lecture made dull by the research he presents.
explanation.definitionFit: Drab means dull and lacking interest, a synonym for tedious or dreary.

clue.text: Rogue trader lurking in harbour area when payment is due

indicators.note: lurking in says the jumbled letters sit inside the harbour word

parts.note: a quay is a landing place in a harbour

indicators.note: rogue as an adjective means behaving wrongly, so the letters of trader go astray into a new order

explanation.surface: A crooked dealer skulking about the docks on the day the money is owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rogue' looks like a noun describing the trader but is the anagram signal; 'lurking in' places the result. Quarter days are the four days a year in England when rents traditionally fall due.
explanation.definitionFit: Quarter days mark the start of each quarter, the traditional dates on which rent and other dues are paid.

clue.text: Dog, not English, quiet and fairly intelligent

indicators.note: not says the English letter is left out

parts.note: the shar-pei is a wrinkled Chinese dog breed
sh is a call for quiet

explanation.surface: A dog that is quiet and fairly clever, not English.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a jokey reading: sharpish means quickly, but read as sharp-ish it is fairly clever.
explanation.definitionFit: Sharp means clever, and the suffix -ish means somewhat, so the word reads as moderately bright.

clue.text: Fashionable fellow back shortly in the city

parts.note: chic means stylish or fashionable
he stands for a man or fellow

indicators.note: shortly says the back word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: the stern is the back of a ship

explanation.surface: A stylish man returning to town before long.
explanation.walkthrough: Chichester is a cathedral city in West Sussex, in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Chichester is a cathedral city in West Sussex, so it is an example of a city.

clue.text: Timber business in outskirts of Chepstow, money spinner

indicators.note: in says the timber and business pieces sit inside those outer letters
outskirts of asks for the first and last letters of Chepstow

parts.note: ash is a timber tree
Co is short for company, a business

explanation.surface: A timber firm near Chepstow that makes lots of money.
explanation.walkthrough: Chepstow is a town in Monmouthshire, Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: A cash cow is a business or product that reliably generates profit, a dependable earner.

clue.text: Headless body a big blow

indicators.note: headless means the body word loses its first letter

parts.note: a dead body is a goner, someone done for

explanation.surface: A headless corpse, the result of a mighty strike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body' here means a corpse, i.e. someone who is a goner. A oner is British slang for a heavy blow or big hit.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a oner is a single heavy punch or hit, a mighty blow that settles things.

clue.text: Ruler's position rising amid ruins of Troy

indicators.note: amid says the reversed position word sits inside the ruined Troy
ruins of says the letters of Troy are wrecked into a new order
rising in a down clue reads the position word upwards

parts.note: a lay is a position or arrangement, as in the lay of the land

explanation.surface: A king's standing rising amid the wreckage of Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruler's position' reads as one phrase, but only 'Ruler's' is the definition, as in a ruler's rank; 'position' starts the wordplay, 'rising' reverses it and 'ruins of' jumbles the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Royalty is the status or rank of a monarch, the quality that belongs to a ruler.

clue.text: Secretary birds soaring over the hill

parts.note: a PA is a personal assistant, a secretary

indicators.note: soaring in a down clue reads the birds word upwards

parts.note: tits are small birds

explanation.surface: A secretary watching birds soar over a hill.
explanation.definitionFit: Past it is an idiom for too old to do something well, the same sense as over the hill.

clue.text: Divers beginning to swim, getting wet?

indicators.note: beginning to asks for the opening letter of the word swim

parts.note: to be getting wet is, whimsically, to be un-drying

explanation.surface: Swimmers starting their swim and soaking themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' looks like people diving but is the old adjective meaning various. The question mark flags the made-up word UNDRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Divers, an old adjective, means several or various of different kinds, just as assorted or miscellaneous do.

clue.text: Teaching gym lesson, love scruffy clothes

parts.note: PE is physical education, the school gym lesson

indicators.note: clothes is a verb here: the scruffy word dresses round the love letter

parts.note: daggy is Australian slang for scruffy or untidy
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O

explanation.surface: A gym class where the teacher wears tatty kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' looks like a noun but is the verb, putting O inside DAGGY.
explanation.definitionFit: Pedagogy is the art, method or practice of instruction, the profession of the classroom teacher.

clue.text: God! Middle East crisis is mounting

indicators.note: mounting in a down clue reads the crisis word upwards

parts.note: the Suez crisis of 1956 was a Middle East conflict over the canal

explanation.surface: An exclamation of alarm as tension grows in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God!' reads as an exclamation; it is the definition, the king of the Greek gods.
explanation.definitionFit: Zeus is the chief god of the Greek pantheon, so he is an example of a deity.

clue.text: Time to have Labour and Tory stalwarts meeting in the middle

parts.note: Con is short for Conservative, the Tory party
stalwarts are fine men, loyal and dependable people

indicators.note: in the middle asks for the central letter of the word meeting

explanation.surface: Labour and Conservative loyalists getting together for talks in the political centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' wants to be the British political party; its capital hides childbirth labour. 'Labour and Tory' reads as a pair, but only 'Tory' is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Confinement is the old term for the period of childbirth, when a mother is in labour and lying in.

clue.text: Half portion of haddock and bread

indicators.note: half portion of says only part of the haddock word is kept, dropping its first three letters

parts.note: finnan, or finnan haddie, is cold-smoked haddock

explanation.surface: A half serving of fish with some bread on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: Finnan haddie is a Scottish smoked haddock.
explanation.definitionFit: Nan, also spelt naan, is a leavened flatbread from South Asian cookery.

clue.text: New drivers encouraged initially to reverse a short distance

indicators.note: to reverse says the learner letters and the opening letter are read backwards

parts.note: L is the learner plate, so two new drivers are two Ls

indicators.note: initially asks for the opening letter of the word encouraged

explanation.surface: Learner drivers being urged to back up a little way.
explanation.walkthrough: An ell is an old measure of cloth, about 45 inches.
explanation.definitionFit: An ell is an old English unit of length for cloth, about forty-five inches, hence a short span.

clue.text: Raises weight by small amounts

parts.note: inches are small amounts, as in moving by inches

explanation.surface: A weightlifter heaving a load up a little at a time.
explanation.definitionFit: To winch is to hoist or lift with a winch, so the verb means lifts or hoists.

clue.text: To agree completely

parts.note: to tally is to agree or correspond, as figures tally

explanation.surface: Agreeing with someone without reservation.
explanation.definitionFit: Totally is an adverb meaning wholly or entirely, the same as fully.
